That’s good news: around 200 million more people are connected than in 2025, the equivalent of almost the entire population of Brazil going online in only one year. But there’s still a long way to go: around 2 billion people remain unconnected. In their official release , ITU Secretary-General Doreen Bogdan-Martin stated: “In the age of AI, being offline means being shut out of countless opportunities, from education to employment. Now more than ever, we need to expand connectivity and make it meaningful for everyone, everywhere.” The Digital Divide Reflects Global Inequality The report highlights how the digital divide reflects other social inequalities , including income, gender, and geography. While 93% of people in high-income countries reported using the Internet, this percentage drops to 32% in low-income countries. That’s also visible across geographies: in Europe, 93% of people are online; in Small Island Developing States (SIDS), it’s 63%; and in Africa, it’s 42%, a record high but still far from the global average. The gender digital divide also persists and varies by region. Globally, 79% of men use the Internet, compared to 74% of women. The Americas are the only region where women (88%) are using the Internet more than men (87%), continuing the trend for the second year in a row. The biggest gap is in low-income countries, where only 28% of women are online, compared with 37% of men. The urban-rural divide is narrowing but remains one of the biggest challenges. While 82% of people living in urban areas use the Internet, only 63% of those living in rural areas have access. The difference is greater in SIDS, with 74% of the urban population connected, compared with only 38% in rural areas. Affordability remains another major barrier, especially for fixed broadband. The ITU evaluates affordability by calculating the cost of a fixed broadband and mobile basket as a percentage of GDP per capita. They define a basket as “the cheapest published non-promotional offering from the Internet service provider with the largest market share using the most common connection technology in the country,” considering at least 5GB of monthly data and a minimum speed of 256 kbit/s. The ITU’s affordability target is 2% of the GDP per capita for the service basket. Globally, the median price is 2.3% for fixed broadband and 1.2% for mobile. The only region meeting the target for fixed broadband is Europe (0.9%). In low-income economies, a fixed broadband subscription can cost the equivalent of more than a quarter of average income. For many people, the cost alone puts connectivity out of reach. The Internet Society Is Working to Change This Addressing global inequality is central to our 2030 Strategy . We believe the Internet is a powerful equalizer that gives people more opportunities to lead healthy and fulfilling lives. We are working to connect the remaining 2 billion people to the Internet and make those connections affordable, reliable, and resilient. Our connectivity work helps communities develop and sustain their own connectivity while strengthening the local Internet infrastructure and policy environments needed to make access affordable, faster, and resilient. That’s why we: Invest and pool resources from partners to fund people and organizations building solutions to close the digital divide and improve Internet affordability and resilience. Provide people with the expertise, data, and technical components they need to establish resilient, affordable Internet access. Advocate for policies that help grow the Internet and support meaningful connectivity. Learn more about our connectivity work and how you can get involved.
